did_you_know.text: The prophecy announces that the end is coming upon the entire land of Israel—“on the four corners of the earth”—emphasizing the widespread extent of the calamity.
The punishment is described as measure for measure: the LORD says He will bring the people’s ways and abominations upon them, so that they may know that He is the LORD.
The word “end” is repeated several times in succession: “An end has come; the end has come,” emphasizing the urgency and nearness of the day of calamity.
Ezekiel uses images of growth to describe the spread of evil: “The rod has blossomed; arrogance has budded”—evil is portrayed as a force that rises and bears fruit.
The calamity disrupts even commercial life: the buyer need not rejoice and the seller need not mourn, because the LORD’s wrath is coming upon the whole multitude.
Although the people blow the trumpet and prepare their weapons for war, no one goes into battle; their military preparations are useless in the face of the LORD’s wrath.
The survivors are described as fleeing to the mountains and moaning like doves in the valleys—a picture that emphasizes fear and each person’s personal grief over his sin.
Silver and gold, normally regarded as sources of security, will not be able to save anyone on the day of the LORD’s wrath. Ezekiel even says they will neither satisfy the soul nor fill the stomach.

The wealth and beauty given to the people for honor were turned into materials for making images of abominations; therefore, those very things become a stumbling block and an object of disgust to them.

During the destruction, a crisis of leadership and guidance arises: the people seek a vision, instruction, and counsel, but the prophet’s vision, the priest’s instruction, and the elders’ counsel are unavailable.
